## Draft — Not Yet Reviewed

This appendix is a work in progress. Content below is subject to revision.
:::

This appendix is an annotated bibliography of freely accessible video lectures, courses, slide decks, and reference guides on literature reviews and evidence synthesis — with and without AI — for readers who want to go deeper than the four chapters of this book. Entries are curated, not exhaustive: each one was picked because it is genuinely free to access, reasonably current, and adds something the others on this list don't. Where a resource carries licensing restrictions (most notably NonCommercial or No-Derivatives Creative Commons terms) or isn't openly licensed at all, that's noted explicitly, since it affects whether you can reuse it in your own teaching versus simply pointing students to it.

## Full Courses and Workshop Materials

- **Evidence Synthesis Institute** — University of Minnesota Libraries, with Cornell. [pressbooks.umn.edu/evidencesynthesisinstitute](https://pressbooks.umn.edu/evidencesynthesisinstitute). Google Slides decks, videos, and per-session resource lists covering the full workflow: question framing → PICO/eligibility → databases → search → grey literature → screening → extraction → risk of bias → PRISMA reporting → protocol registration. CC BY-NC 4.0 — the only openly-licensed, *editable* slide set covering the whole process end to end. Framed for library-support staff, so expect to add your own AI-specific content; NonCommercial licensing means you can adapt it for teaching but not resell it.
- **Systematic Review & Mapping Methods Course** — Neal Haddaway, Stockholm Environment Institute. [systematicreviewmethods.github.io](https://systematicreviewmethods.github.io). Thirteen modules of recorded lectures, readings, and practical exercises, discipline-neutral rather than health-specific, and unusual in dedicating whole modules to narrative and qualitative synthesis. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 — share and stream freely, but the No-Derivatives term means you can't edit or re-cut the material into your own slides.
- **Systematic Reviews: The Essentials (Part 1)** — Christine Neilson & Janice Linton, University of Manitoba Libraries. YouTube, ~60 minutes, 2023. A thorough librarian-led workshop covering the whole review pipeline from question to citation management. Health-sciences framed but the underlying process transfers to other fields; long enough that assigning select sections works better than the full hour.
- **A Guide to Evidence Synthesis** — Cornell University Library. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Not a lecture but a step-by-step, tool-linked practical reference (protocol → databases → grey literature → search → registration → screening → risk of bias → extraction → synthesis), plus a curated list of open-access tools. Useful to keep open *while actually doing* a review, rather than as a one-off watch.

## Short Video Lectures and Tutorials

- **Literature Reviews: An Overview for Graduate Students** — John Classen, NC State University Libraries. ~15 minutes, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0. A concise, openly-licensed introduction distinguishing selective from comprehensive reviews and walking through topic selection, searching, evaluating, and writing. The Creative Commons license makes this one of the few videos on this list you can legally embed directly in your own course materials.
- **How to Conduct a Systematic Review… 7 Steps (with PRISMA, PICO & AI)** — Dr. Amina Yonis. YouTube, ~18 minutes. A clear step-by-step tutorial covering PICO question framing and the PRISMA flow, with explicit mentions of AI tools for search and screening. Standard YouTube license (not CC) — fine to link and cite, not to redistribute.
- **How to Automate Your Literature Review Ethically (Using ChatGPT)** — Prof. David Stuckler, University of Oxford. YouTube, ~20 minutes, 2023. A hands-on demonstration of using ChatGPT for brainstorming, drafting, and keyword generation, paired explicitly with its failure modes — fabricated citations, shallow synthesis. One of the few widely-available lectures that teaches critical, disclosed AI use rather than either avoidance or blind reliance; a natural companion to [Chapter 3](ch03-chapter-three.qmd) and [Chapter 4](ch04-chapter-four.qmd) of this book.
- **Systemaattinen kirjallisuuskatsaus: suunnittelu, toteutus ja raportointi** ["Systematic Literature Review: Planning, Implementation and Reporting"] — Minna Stolt, University of Turku / Satakunta Wellbeing Region. Slide deck (PDF), 44 slides, in Finnish, presented February 2025. [satainno.fi PDF](https://satainno.fi/wp-content/uploads/Kirjallisuuskatsaus-Stolt_2025.pdf). A concise, practically-oriented walkthrough of the systematic-review process — planning, databases and search terms, screening, data analysis, reporting — aimed at nursing-science researchers but generalizable to other fields. Useful specifically for Finnish-speaking readers who want the same fundamentals covered in Chapter 2 explained in their first language.
- **PRISMA Flow Diagram Tutorial** — Five Minute Friday. YouTube, ~5 minutes, 2024. A very short, focused demo of filling in a PRISMA flow diagram — a quick visual aid rather than a standalone lesson, best used alongside one of the fuller resources above.

## AI in Evidence Synthesis — Dedicated Resources

- **"AI methods in evidence synthesis" Learning Live series** — Cochrane, with Cochrane Germany / University of Freiburg. [training.cochrane.org/node/2287](https://training.cochrane.org/node/2287). Webinar recordings plus downloadable slide PDFs, six sessions of roughly one hour each, 2024–2025. Covers AI in searching, screening, data extraction, and writing, including a dedicated "responsible AI / RAISE" session, presented by named methodologists rather than a vendor. The single best free, critically-framed resource on AI in evidence synthesis available today — the natural next stop after Chapters 3 and 4 of this book. Free to view and download, but not formally open-licensed.
- **ASReview LAB teaching materials** — Utrecht University. [asreview.nl](https://asreview.nl). Documentation, tutorials, videos, and a presentation handout for ASReview, the open-source active-learning screening tool referenced throughout Chapter 3. Apache 2.0 for the software; the handout is freely available. Built explicitly around reproducibility and FAIR data — the best hands-on example of a transparent, auditable AI workflow rather than a black box.
- **AI in Evidence Synthesis (Elicit overview)** — Lambert et al., open-access article via PMC, CC BY. Not a lecture, but a short, freely-reusable article summarizing Elicit's GPT-based semantic search approach and its coverage and reliability limitations — a compact supplementary reading rather than a video, and a useful pairing with [Chapter 3's evidence on Elicit](ch03-chapter-three.qmd#ai-use-across-the-12-steps).

## Reference Guides and Reporting Standards

- **PRISMA 2020 statement, checklists & flow diagrams** — PRISMA / EQUATOR Network. [prisma-statement.org/prisma-2020](https://prisma-statement.org/prisma-2020). Checklists in PDF/Word, flow diagrams, and a Shiny app for building one interactively. The checklists themselves are CC BY 4.0 — the most freely reusable single asset on this entire list, and the reporting standard underlying [Chapter 2's Step 11](ch02-chapter-two.qmd#the-12-steps-of-a-literature-review) and [Chapter 3's Step 11](ch03-chapter-three.qmd#ai-use-across-the-12-steps).
- **Systematic reviews — for researchers** — Karolinska Institutet University Library. [kib.ki.se](https://kib.ki.se/en/search-evaluate/systematic-reviews). Web guidance with an evidence-pyramid graphic and workflow overview, written directly for doctoral-level researchers. A concise Nordic reference point in English, useful alongside Stolt's Finnish-language slides above.
- **Cochrane–Campbell–JBI–CEE Position Statement on AI, and the RAISE recommendations** — Flemyng et al. (2025), [doi.org/10.1186/s13750-025-00374-5](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13750-025-00374-5). Open-access article, CC BY, roughly an hour to read. The current authoritative, cross-organizational governance statement on AI use in evidence synthesis — already cited throughout Chapters 2 through 4 of this book, and included here again as the single most important follow-up reading if you read nothing else on this list.
